name: Leptos
vendor: Greg Johnston and the Leptos contributors
summary: A full-stack Rust web framework: components compile to WebAssembly for the browser and to a native server binary, with fine-grained signals that update single DOM nodes and server functions that replace a hand-written API.
intro: A Leptos app is written entirely in Rust. Components are functions that return a view, written with the JSX-like `view!` macro, and state lives in signals: `let (count, set_count) = signal(0);`. A component runs once. It creates the real DOM nodes and sets up effects that depend on the signals they read, so when `count` changes, only the text node that shows it is updated: there is no virtual DOM to diff and no component re-render. Leptos is closest to SolidJS in JavaScript and Sycamore in Rust.

The browser half is compiled to WebAssembly for the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target. A client-side app is built with Trunk and served as a single-page app. A full-stack app is built with `cargo-leptos`, which compiles the same crate twice: a native server, on Axum or Actix, that renders HTML and streams it to the browser, and a Wasm bundle that hydrates that HTML into a live app. Islands mode goes further and ships Wasm only for components marked `#[island]`; the guide’s demo shrank from about 274 KB of Wasm to about 24 KB. A `#[server]` function becomes an HTTP endpoint in the server build and, in the browser build, a stub that serializes the arguments and calls it, so database queries can sit next to the components that use them. The current stable line is 0.8; 0.9 is at its first release candidate.
strengths: Fine-grained updates: a changed signal touches one text node or class, without re-running components or diffing a virtual DOM
One language and one type system from database to DOM, with server functions instead of a separately maintained REST API
Server rendering with streaming HTML and hydration, and islands mode to ship Wasm only for the interactive parts
Runs as a static front end inside Tauri for desktop and mobile apps
limits: Still 0.x: each minor release can break APIs, and 0.7 rewrote the framework’s internals
Server functions are a public HTTP API in disguise: anything they return is exposed, so they need the same authentication and rate limits as any endpoint
Everything goes through Rust compile times, and the browser must download and compile a Wasm binary before the page becomes interactive
Inside Tauri only a static front end works, since Tauri doesn’t officially support server-based setups, so server rendering and server functions are left out

story: Rust could already run in browsers through WebAssembly, and Yew, an earlier Rust framework, used a virtual DOM: state changes re-run components, which produce a new virtual tree to diff against the old one. Greg Johnston, who describes himself as a classicist, started Leptos in 2022 under the influence of SolidJS instead, and named it after the Greek λεπτός, “thin, light, refined, fine-grained”. Version 0.1 came out in January 2023.

Leptos grew into a full-stack framework: server rendering with streaming, hydration, a router and isomorphic server functions, which Dioxus also uses in its full-stack mode. Version 0.7, in November 2024, was a nearly complete rewrite of the internals after more than a year of work, aimed at smaller Wasm binaries, faster HTML rendering, better async support and signals that can cross threads. 0.8 followed in May 2025, and 0.9 reached its first release candidate in October 2026, promising that most 0.8 code upgrades without changes.

choices.choice: Fine-grained signals instead of a virtual DOM
choices.why: Re-running a component and diffing its output costs work on every change. Running components once and wiring signals to the exact DOM nodes that read them means a change touches only those nodes.
Server-only logic such as database queries and authentication can live beside the components that use it, called like a local async function, without designing and maintaining a separate REST API.

Suspense had edge cases, Wasm binaries and HTML were larger than they needed to be, and signals couldn’t be sent across threads; the rewrite fixed these while keeping most application code compatible.
